decks.module: Good habits and getting under way
decks.domain: Driving habits, turns, bicycles and motorcycles

cards.front: What qualities and habits does the manual say make a safe driver?
cards.back: A safe driver knows and respects the rules, follows proper procedures, keeps a good attitude and is courteous at all times, using good habits on every trip, short or long.

cards.front: What should you do after getting in the car and before switching on the ignition?
cards.back: On entering the car, adjust the seat and mirrors, make sure passengers are seated so they will not interfere, and buckle up with every passenger before switching on the ignition.

cards.front: How do you start a manual car compared with an automatic?
cards.back: With a manual transmission push in the clutch before turning the key; with an automatic, have the indicator in park or neutral and press the brake as you turn the key.
cards.memory_hook: clutch in, or park and brake

cards.front: How should you sit and hold the steering wheel?
cards.back: Sit upright and grip the outside rim with both hands, firm enough for control but not so tight it slows your reflexes, removing a hand only to signal or operate the vehicle.

cards.front: How do you pull out of a parallel parking space?
cards.back: To leave a parallel parking space, look over your shoulder and in the mirrors, wait until clear, signal, and enter the nearest lane, staying there until a lane change is safe.

cards.front: What does the law say about keeping to a lane?
cards.back: You must keep within a single lane, never weaving between lanes or straddling the lane marking.

cards.front: What counts as a traffic lane?
cards.back: A traffic lane is any part of a road wide enough for a vehicle or line of vehicles to travel safely, and it exists whether or not it is marked.
cards.memory_hook: marked or not, still a lane

decks.domain: Driving habits, turns, bicycles and motorcycles

cards.front: When should you plan a turn and move into the turn lane?
cards.back: Plan each turn early rather than at the last moment, and move into the proper turn lane well before it once the change is safe.

cards.front: How far before a turn must you signal, and for how long?
cards.back: Signal at least one hundred feet before turning and keep the signal on until you actually turn, so both pedestrians and drivers know your intention.

cards.front: Where do your hands go during a turn, and who has the right of way?
cards.back: Both hands belong on the wheel during the turn itself, and pedestrians have the right of way over motor vehicles.

cards.front: What steps make up a safe turn from start to finish?
cards.back: Slow down before turning, check front, rear and sides for cars and pedestrians, finish in the proper lane, and cancel the signal afterward.

cards.front: Why may you add hand and arm signals in daylight?
cards.back: In daylight you may add hand and arm signals to your signal lights, because bright sunlight can make a flashing signal hard to see.

cards.front: How do you make a right turn from a four-lane or divided highway?
cards.back: For a right turn from a four-lane or divided highway, get into the right lane well ahead and turn tightly into the right lane of the cross street.
cards.memory_hook: right lane in, right lane out

cards.front: How do you make a left turn from a four-lane or divided highway?
cards.back: For a left turn there, move to the lane nearest the center line or divider, turn from the inside lane without a wide swing, and enter just right of the cross street's center line, unless signs or markings allow turns from more lanes.

cards.front: How does lane choice differ for right and left turns from a four-lane highway?
cards.back: A right turn from a four-lane highway starts in the right lane and ends tight in the cross street's right lane, while a left turn starts from the inside lane nearest the center line.
cards.memory_hook: right from right, left from inside

cards.front: When does the turn signal go on, and when does it go off?
cards.back: Turn signals go on at least one hundred feet before the turn and kept on until you turn, and then must be switched off once the maneuver is complete.

cards.front: Do hand and arm signals replace signal lights in daylight?
cards.back: Signal lights are the standard turn signal, and hand and arm signals are an addition for daylight when sunlight can wash out the light, not a replacement.

decks.domain: Driving habits, turns, bicycles and motorcycles

cards.front: When is a three-point turn normally allowed?
cards.back: A three-point turn reverses your direction and must not endanger other traffic, so it is normally allowed only where you can be seen from far away and traffic makes it safe.

cards.front: Where are three-point turns banned?
cards.back: Three-point turns are banned on interstate freeways, on curves, and near hilltops where drivers approaching within five hundred feet from either direction cannot see you.

cards.front: Who governs three-point turns, and will there always be a sign?
cards.back: Local ordinances govern three-point turns, there may be no warning signs, and prohibiting signs are usually posted only at hazardous spots.

cards.front: Can a three-point turn be prohibited where no sign forbids it?
cards.back: Three-point turns are prohibited where oncoming drivers within five hundred feet cannot see you, even when no sign forbids the turn.

cards.front: How should you enter and drive through a curve?
cards.back: Slow down before a curve so you do not cross the center line or leave the road, entering slowly enough to accelerate slightly while rounding it.

decks.domain: Driving habits, turns, bicycles and motorcycles

cards.front: What road rights and duties do people on bicycles have?
cards.back: People on bicycles have the same road rights and responsibilities as people in motor vehicles, so drivers and cyclists alike must know and obey state traffic laws.

cards.front: Where does a cyclist ride on a roadway, and when may the rider move left?
cards.back: A cyclist on a roadway rides as close as practicable to the right curb or edge, except when passing, preparing a left turn, or avoiding hazards such as debris, opening car doors or pedestrians.
cards.memory_hook: keep right unless passing or avoiding

cards.front: May cyclists ride two abreast, and which direction must they ride?
cards.back: People on bicycles may ride two abreast at all times, and they must ride with the flow of traffic.

cards.front: How can cyclists keep right yet still ride two abreast or move left?
cards.back: Cyclists normally keep as far right as practicable, yet they may also ride two abreast at all times and move left to pass, to turn left, or to avoid hazards.

cards.front: How do cyclists signal turns, lane changes and stops?
cards.back: Cyclists signal turns, lane changes and stops with the same hand and arm signals that drivers use.

cards.front: Where must cyclists ride when there is a bicycle lane, and may they use sidewalks?
cards.back: Cyclists must use a bicycle lane where one exists; sidewalks and multipurpose paths are not bicycle lanes, and riding a bicycle on the sidewalk is illegal in Alabama.

cards.front: Which cyclists must wear helmets, and where?
cards.back: Cyclists under sixteen must wear a securely fastened helmet on public roads, other public rights-of-way, public bicycle paths and in public parks.

cards.front: When may a driver enter a bicycle lane?
cards.back: A driver may enter a bicycle lane only to park where parking is allowed, to enter or leave the highway, or to prepare for a turn.

cards.front: How do you turn across a bicycle lane?
cards.back: To turn across a bicycle lane, move into the lane before the turn, but only when doing so does not endanger a cyclist using it.

cards.front: What are a driver's only reasons to use a bicycle lane, and how is a turn across it made?
cards.back: Drivers stay out of bicycle lanes except to park, enter or leave the highway, or prepare a turn, and for a turn across the lane they move into it first when it is safe.

decks.domain: Driving habits, turns, bicycles and motorcycles

cards.front: How much room must you leave when passing a cyclist, and why?
cards.back: Alabama law requires at least three feet between your vehicle and a person on a bicycle when you pass, and wind from fast vehicles can push a cyclist enough to cause a crash.

cards.front: Who does the helmet rule cover compared with the passing clearance rule?
cards.back: The bicycle helmet rule applies to riders under sixteen, while the three-foot passing clearance applies to every driver passing any cyclist.

cards.front: Where should you avoid passing a cyclist?
cards.back: Avoid passing a cyclist uphill, on curves, where visibility is limited, or when other vehicles occupy the lane you would need to use.

cards.front: What should you do when a narrow road makes passing a cyclist unsafe?
cards.back: When a narrow road makes passing unsafe, stay a safe distance behind the cyclist, without tailgating or blasting the horn, until you can pass.

cards.front: Where should you watch most closely for cyclists?
cards.back: Watch closely for cyclists at intersections, when crossing sidewalks, and when entering or leaving alleys or driveways.

cards.front: How does wet weather affect a bicycle's braking?
cards.back: A bicycle brakes far less well in wet weather, so drivers should allow for its reduced ability to slow or stop.

cards.front: What should bicycles carry at night, and what should drivers do?
cards.back: State law says bicycles should carry lights or reflectors for night riding, and drivers need extra caution in darkness or poor visibility.

decks.domain: Driving habits, turns, bicycles and motorcycles

cards.front: What rights do motorcyclists have, and who is in many motorcycle crashes?
cards.back: Motorcyclists share the same road rights and responsibilities as other users, and a substantial share of motorcycle crashes involve riders with limited experience.

cards.front: Why is a motorcycle hard to see and judge?
cards.back: A motorcycle is only about two feet wide against a car's five to six feet, so it is hard to pick out and its distance and speed are hard to judge.
cards.memory_hook: two feet wide, hard to judge

cards.front: What should you do before turning left in front of an oncoming motorcycle?
cards.back: Left turns in front of an oncoming motorcycle cause a large share of car-motorcycle injury crashes, so look twice and know the motorcycle's speed before you turn left.

cards.front: Why is seeing a motorcycle not enough before a left turn?
cards.back: Seeing a motorcycle is not enough before a left turn, because drivers also misjudge its distance and speed, so look again and know its speed first.

cards.front: What must you check before turning in front of a vehicle with its signal on?
cards.back: Before turning in front of any vehicle, make sure it is really turning and not going straight with a forgotten signal still blinking.

cards.front: What following distance should you leave behind a motorcycle?
cards.back: Leave the same two-second following distance behind a motorcycle as behind any vehicle, since tailgating can distract the rider.

cards.front: May a car share a lane with a motorcycle?
cards.back: A motorcycle is entitled to a full lane, and a driver must never pull alongside it in the same lane, even a wide one, which is illegal and very dangerous.

cards.front: Does a rider's position within the lane change the full-lane rule?
cards.back: A motorcyclist changing position within the lane is still using a full lane, so a car may never share that lane even when the rider is far to one side.

cards.front: When should you give motorcycles even more following distance?
cards.back: Give motorcycles even more following distance in darkness, rain or on wet, slippery roads, and watch for rain glare that can hide a rider at night.

cards.front: How does following distance behind a motorcycle change in bad conditions?
cards.back: Behind a motorcycle the normal gap is the same two seconds as behind a car, but in darkness, rain or on slippery roads the gap should be longer.

cards.front: What wind and road conditions can make a motorcyclist suddenly change speed or direction?
cards.back: Crosswinds on open highways and bridges, windblasts from fast large trucks, and road hazards such as gravel, seams, manhole covers, rough rail crossings or metal bridges can make a rider suddenly change speed or direction.

recaps.module: Good habits and getting under way

recap_hooks.text: Adjust and buckle up before the ignition, hold the wheel with both hands, and keep to one lane, marked or not.
Plan turns early, signal at least one hundred feet ahead, and cancel the signal once the turn is done.
Turn right from the right lane into the right lane, and left from the inside lane without a wide swing.
Three-point turns need long sight lines and are banned on freeways, curves and blind hilltops, sign or no sign.
Cyclists share the road, keep right with exceptions, may ride two abreast, and use bicycle lanes; riders under sixteen wear helmets.
Give every cyclist at least three feet when passing, and hang back when passing is unsafe.
Look twice and judge a motorcycle's speed before a left turn, leave at least two seconds, and never share its lane.
